panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: AP radiograph of the left great toe shows a phalangeal lytic lesion with cortical scalloping and chondroid calcification; caption and case report support solitary enchondroma in an adolescent. B: Oblique/lateral radiograph of the same left great toe shows the phalangeal lytic lesion with cortical scalloping and calcification; findings and article context support solitary enchondroma.
panels.attribution_text: Patel et al. A Solitary Enchondroma of the Great Toe in an Adolescent Male: A Case Report.. Cureus 2022. doi:10.7759/cureus.21772. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: X-ray showing lytic lesions, scalloping of the cortex, and whorls of calcification.
in_text_mentions: ular swelling over the dorsal aspect of the left great toe, which was hard in consistency without any neurovascular impairment, were observed. No presence of scars, sinuses, pigmentation, or any ulceration was observed over the swelling. Palpation of the swelling confirmed the presence of a bony hard swelling, nonpedunculated, and smooth surface of size 3 × 3 × 2.5 cm with ill-defined margins. The swelling was expansile and fixed to the skin. X-ray (Figure 1) and MRI (Figures 2A, 2B) were performed for further evaluation. The core needle biopsy was performed, which was suggestive of chondroma.

panels.rationale: Single histology panel (H&E) of an intraoperative sample; caption and in-text describe an enchondroma comprising locules of hyaline cartilage. Article title specifies an adolescent male with solitary enchondroma of the great toe. No skin, ethnicity, or stage information is present.
panels.attribution_text: Patel et al. A Solitary Enchondroma of the Great Toe in an Adolescent Male: A Case Report.. Cureus 2022. doi:10.7759/cureus.21772. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathological examination of the intraoperative sample suggestive of enchondroma.
in_text_mentions: Histopathological examination (Figure 4) of the intraoperative sample was suggestive of enchondroma tumor comprising locules of the hyaline cartilage separated from the bone marrow. Postoperative X-ray was performed (Figure 5A), and the patient was placed on a below-knee POP (plaster of Paris) slab and non-weight-bearing for 12 weeks. Regular follow-up was performed, and an X-ray was taken at regular intervals (Figures 5B, 5C). At the two-year follow-up, the patient was fine without signs of recurrence.
